title: Your Platform Was Built For A Different Era, And AI Just Exposed It
gist: Broadcom's senior director of private cloud solutions argues that internal developer platforms — now used by 90 percent of organizations per Google's 2025 DORA research — were built for human developers shipping containers and are structurally unready for GPU provisioning, AI agents as non-human users, and token-level cost control. He pitches 'Platform Engineering 2.0' as a five-pillar evolution (AI-native/Agentic Development Platform, multi-persona, embedded FinOps, security shifted down, composable) rather than a rebuild, with AI-native readiness as the 12-month milestone. Note: this is explicitly sponsored content for Broadcom and its Platform Engineering 2.0 whitepaper, so the framing is vendor-shaped.

themes.theme: Platform Adoption Is Saturated, Fitness Is Not

insights.claim: Google's 2025 DORA research found 90 percent of organizations now report using an internal platform and 76 percent have established dedicated platform teams, meaning the enterprise platform-adoption TAM is largely saturated and future vendor growth must come from upgrade/replacement cycles rather than greenfield land-grabs.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Gupta
insights.so_what: Platform-tooling vendors selling first-time adoption face a shrinking pool; the investable motion shifts to modernization/refresh revenue and displacement of incumbent internal stacks.
insights.quote: Google’s 2025 DORA research found that 90 percent of organizations now report using an internal platform, and 76 percent have established dedicated platform teams.
insights.locator: The debate about whether enterprises need

insights.claim: Existing developer platforms fail at three specific infrastructure primitives — provisioning GPUs on demand, governing AI agents, and enforcing cost control at the moment of provisioning — because the substrate underneath them was designed developer-centric rather than accelerator- or agent-aware.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Gupta
insights.so_what: Names the exact three feature gaps that platform vendors will race to fill; useful as a due-diligence checklist when evaluating IDP/DevOps tooling companies.
insights.quote: the developer-centric substrate that was never designed to provision GPUs on demand, govern AI agents, or enforce cost control at the moment of provisioning
insights.locator: At the base of every crack is infrastructure

themes.theme: Bottleneck Migration From Authoring To Delivery

insights.claim: With AI coding assistants now mainstream, the software bottleneck has moved from writing code to delivering it, because CI/CD pipelines were never sized for the volume of machine-generated code organizations can now produce and review.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Gupta
insights.so_what: Demand should rotate from code-generation tools toward build, test, release and review infrastructure — the throughput layer is the new constraint and the new spend.
insights.quote: The bottleneck has moved. It is no longer about writing code – it is about delivering it.
insights.locator: Most developers are now using AI coding assistants

insights.claim: The developer role has shifted from author of code to reviewer and orchestrator of machine-generated work, which changes what tooling developers actually need and what seat-based productivity metrics measure.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Gupta
insights.so_what: Review, provenance and orchestration tooling becomes the growth category; per-seat authoring tools risk commoditization.
insights.quote: the developer’s job has quietly changed from author to reviewer and orchestrator of machine-generated work
insights.locator: Your pipelines were never sized for that throughput

themes.theme: The Agent As A Non-Human Platform User

insights.claim: AI agents constitute a new class of platform user requiring authentication, token usage regulation at both organization and user level, GPU allocation, MCP compatibility, scoped permissions, non-human identity, audit logging and hard guardrails — and most existing platforms have no native answer for any of it.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Gupta
insights.so_what: This is the concrete requirements list for the agent-governance software category; non-human identity and MCP gateways are the near-term procurement lines to watch.
insights.quote: Agents need authentication, token usage regulation and management at an organization and user level, GPU allocation, MCP compatibility, scoped permissions, non-human identity, audit logging, and hard guardrails on what they’re allowed to do.
insights.locator: Then there’s a brand-new kind of user knocking on the door

insights.claim: Platform teams that built golden paths for developer autonomy are now being handed responsibility for enterprise-wide agentic autonomy, which the author calls the largest mandate the platform engineering discipline has ever held.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Gupta
insights.so_what: Budget authority for agent governance is likely to consolidate inside platform teams rather than security or data-science orgs — sell and staff accordingly.
insights.quote: That’s the largest mandate the discipline has ever held.
insights.locator: The teams that built golden paths for developer autonomy

insights.claim: Broadcom's Private Cloud Outlook 2026 study reports 97 percent of IT leaders believe some public cloud spend is wasted and 52 percent estimate the waste exceeds 25 percent of their total public cloud budget.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Gupta
insights.so_what: A vendor-sourced but quotable number underpinning repatriation and private-cloud pitches; treat the framing as interested since Broadcom sponsors the piece.
insights.quote: 97 percent of IT leaders believe some of their public cloud spend is wasted, and 52 percent estimate that waste exceeds 25 percent of their total public cloud budget
insights.locator: Cost is the third pressure

insights.claim: The per-prompt and per-retry token cost of AI workloads is a spending category most existing cost-reporting tools simply cannot see, leaving a measurement blind spot on top of GPU, inference-endpoint and training spend that already dwarfs traditional cloud consumption.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Gupta
insights.so_what: Open whitespace for token-level cost attribution products; incumbent cloud-cost vendors that cannot instrument tokens face displacement risk.
insights.quote: On top sits the token cost of every prompt and retry – a category most cost-reporting tools simply can’t see.
insights.locator: AI infrastructure makes it dramatically worse

insights.claim: Retrospective FinOps built on monthly reviews and quarterly cleanup sprints is structurally obsolete for AI because a single misconfigured AI workload can burn through the budget overnight, forcing cost decisions to move to provisioning time.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Gupta
insights.so_what: The FinOps product category has to shift from reporting to real-time enforcement; report-only vendors are the ones exposed.
insights.quote: Retrospective FinOps, the monthly review and quarterly cleanup sprint, can’t catch a misconfigured AI workload that burns through budget overnight.
insights.locator: Cost is the third pressure

themes.theme: New Attack Surfaces And Security Shifted Down

insights.claim: AI introduces attack surfaces — shadow AI sprawl, prompt injection, model poisoning and inference data leaks — that no SAST or DAST scan in an existing pipeline was built to detect, while the EU AI Act, US executive orders and data residency rules keep adding compliance load.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Gupta
insights.so_what: Legacy application-security scanning has a coverage hole around AI; AI-specific security and sovereignty tooling is a distinct budget line, not an upsell to existing AppSec.
insights.quote: AI introduces new vast attack surfaces – shadow AI sprawl, prompt injection, model poisoning, inference data leaks – that no SAST or DAST scan in your pipeline was built to detect.
insights.locator: Privacy, security and sovereignty round out the list

insights.claim: Shift-left security moved scanning earlier but merely dumped the load onto developers while most vulnerabilities still surface in production, so security should instead 'shift down' into the platform and runtime layers where it is invisible to developers and immutable by design.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Gupta
insights.so_what: A directional call against a decade of shift-left orthodoxy; favors runtime/platform-embedded security vendors over developer-facing scanner businesses.
insights.quote: Shift-left moved security earlier in the pipeline but dumped the load onto developers, and most vulnerabilities still surface in production.
insights.locator: Fourth, security shifts down

themes.theme: Platform Engineering 2.0 As Extension, Not Rebuild

insights.claim: Platform Engineering 2.0 is framed as an extension of existing foundations — Platform as Product, golden paths, shift-left security, self-service IDPs — across five pillars rather than a rebuild, explicitly telling buyers not to tear up what they have.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Gupta
insights.so_what: A low-friction upgrade narrative is easier to sell into constrained budgets than rip-and-replace, which favors incumbents with installed platform bases.
insights.quote: The discipline doesn’t reset at each phase. It evolves.
insights.locator: Platform Engineering 2.0 Evolution, Not A Rebuild

insights.claim: The Internal Developer Platform is being renamed and repositioned as an Agentic Development Platform (ADP) that treats AI workloads as first-class citizens and AI agents as first-class users while keeping the same operating model.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Gupta
insights.so_what: Watch for 'ADP' as an emerging analyst category label — category creation usually precedes a pricing and positioning reset in the tooling market.
insights.quote: Your IDP evolves into what’s increasingly being called an Agentic Development Platform (ADP)
insights.locator: The first pillar is an AI-native platform

insights.claim: Most platforms serve application developers well and treat security teams, data scientists, ML engineers, FinOps analysts, business leaders and agents as second-class citizens, leaving significant unrealized value that a multi-persona experience on shared APIs would capture.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Gupta
insights.so_what: Multi-persona expansion is the seat-count expansion story for platform vendors — more internal buyers per deployed platform.
insights.locator: Second, is a multi-persona experience

insights.claim: Embedded FinOps makes every developer a FinOps practitioner by default not through training but because the platform surfaces cost at the moment of action, moving cost governance from rear-view-mirror reporting into the provisioning path.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Gupta
insights.so_what: Cost controls that live in the provisioning workflow are stickier and harder to displace than dashboards — a moat characteristic worth pricing in.
insights.quote: Every developer becomes a FinOps practitioner by default – not through training, but because the platform surfaces cost at the moment of action.
insights.locator: Third, is embedded FinOps

insights.claim: The CNCF projects ecosystem has grown from roughly 50 projects in 2018 to more than 200 today, and that expanding choice surface is the stated reason rigid, non-composable platforms cannot keep pace.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Gupta
insights.so_what: Fragmentation of the cloud-native stack favors API-first swappable components and penalizes monolithic suite vendors — a headwind for bundled platform pricing.
insights.quote: The CNCF projects ecosystem has grown from about 50 projects in 2018 to more than 200 today; rigid platforms can’t keep pace with that choice surface.
insights.locator: Fifth, composable by design

insights.claim: The fifth pillar reframes build-versus-buy as compose: API-first, swappable building blocks that let an organization replace one CI/CD tool or observability stack without cascading changes.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Gupta
insights.so_what: Lower switching costs across the stack compress vendor lock-in and pressure renewal pricing for point tools.
insights.quote: The future isn’t build versus buy – it’s compose.
insights.locator: Fifth, composable by design

themes.theme: Twelve-Month Readiness Test And Vendor Framing

insights.claim: The stated 12-month milestone that matters most is AI-native readiness defined as five concrete capabilities: GPU workload support, agents, non-human identity, token economics, and MCP gateway exposure.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Gupta
insights.so_what: A concrete near-term roadmap checklist to score enterprise-software vendors and internal platform teams against over the next year.
insights.quote: GPU workload support; agents; non-human identity; token economics; and MCP gateway exposure
insights.locator: Where To Start: AI Native Platform Readiness

insights.claim: The recommended audit is a three-gap test of the current IDP — GPU/accelerator provisioning, non-human identity management, and real-time cost attribution at provisioning time — with the assertion that a platform missing all three is already behind.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Gupta
insights.so_what: A fast, three-question diagnostic usable in diligence calls to separate AI-ready platform assets from legacy DevOps tooling.
insights.quote: If all three are missing, your platform is already behind.
insights.locator: Start by auditing your current IDP for three gaps

insights.claim: The entire Platform Engineering 2.0 framework is sponsored content authored by Broadcom's senior director of private cloud solutions and points readers to a Broadcom and Platformengineering.org whitepaper, and its supporting cost statistic also comes from Broadcom's own Private Cloud Outlook 2026 study.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Gupta
insights.so_what: Discount the urgency framing accordingly: Broadcom/VMware benefits directly if enterprises conclude their platforms need an AI-native private-cloud refresh.
insights.quote: This content was sponsored by Broadcom.
insights.locator: Pankaj Gupta is senior director of private cloud solutions at Broadcom
